scope: Read-only bounded primary-source screen; derivations marked [INFERENCE]; ran nothing.

output.summary: I read about 20 primary sources on 2026-10-19 and ran nothing. Main result: no source proves a quantum Hall–Paige theorem. In particular, none rules out an unrestricted QLS orthogonal to B = Cay(Z_10) or Cay(D_5), or to Cay(Z_8), or to the table of any group whose Sylow 2-subgroup is cyclic and nontrivial. I also found no explicit QLS mate for any Latin square that lacks a classical mate. So the fixed-B route is not excluded, but it has no precedent. Not finding a no-go does not guarantee headroom. Evidence against: (i) every orthogonal pair (2-MOQLS) of order 4 or 5 is classical, and none exists at order 6 (Ball–Simoens), so Cay(Z_2), Cay(Z_4), Cay(Z_6) and Cay(S_3) have no quantum mate. (ii) Every structured sub-class at v=10 that I checked is ruled out. That covers the WH10 single orbit (parent, Grassl et al.) and the whole Árnadóttir–Roberson (G,G)-invariant class, which contains every Huang–Li, Zhang–Cao and Ball–Simoens construction; it fails for Z_n with n even and for D_5 [INFERENCE]. It also covers the parent's FCO row-relabelled family: the parent's enumeration found 0 at n=10 and n=8, and I give a short proof for every n=2p with p an odd prime [INFERENCE, unreviewed]. FCO is the same thing as a spectral pair of two permutation graphs in Z_n^2, or a Butson Hadamard matrix ζ^{it+ρ(i)π(t)} of mod-n rank ≤2 (Kolountzakis–Matolcsi dictionary). Iosevich–Mayeli–Pakianathan (IMP) plus Rédei's bound reproduce the parent's n=7 count of 198 exactly [INFERENCE]. Fallon–Kiss–Somlai (Fuglede's conjecture holds in Z_pq^2, which includes Z_10^2) does not give the FCO no-go, because permutation graphs always tile. No source states the FCO no-go. I started no processes and own no live children, in line with the parent HOLD.

findings.claim: Maximal 1-RQLS(10) is one of the 17 open orders, all ≡ 2 mod 4. Every construction route in the paper stops exactly at v ≡ 2 mod 4: Construction 3.3 needs a complete mapping of Z2×Zm with m even, and Lemma 3.5 needs m = 2k ≥ 6. Open status is not a no-go, and it concerns any B, not a fixed Cayley B.
findings.quote: For any integer v ≥ 7 and v ∉ {10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 38, 42, 46, 54, 58, 62, 66, 74, 82, 94}, there exists a 1-RQLS(v) with maximal cardinality.
findings.source: Zhang & Cao, Resolvable quantum Latin squares with maximal cardinality
findings.read_scope: Full arXiv PDF text: Thm 1.3, §2 (Lemma 2.2, Ex. 2.4), §3 (Constr. 3.3, Lemmas 3.4–3.5), §4 proof table, §5. The page-5 table came through garbled; symbols normalized.
findings.scope: Existence for some B. v ≡ 2 mod 4 left open.

findings.claim: Lemma 2.2: a t-RQLS is the same as a QLS plus t classical MOQLS partners. So the target is exactly 'a QLS orthogonal (tensor-ONB sense) to a fixed classical B'. The small-order facts imported from Ball–Simoens sit in §2, just before Ex. 2.4; the proposal cites §3. Ex. 2.4's v=8 maximal example has transversals j = i XOR c, so B = Cay(Z2^3), which has classical mates.
findings.quote: Therefore, by Lemma 2.2, every 1-RQLS(v) is classical for v ∈ {4, 5} and hence has cardinality v, while no 1-RQLS(6) exists.
findings.source: Zhang & Cao 2608.29201v2
findings.scope: Rules out even cyclic Cayley tables at orders 2, 4, 6 only.

findings.claim: There are no non-entangled 2-MOQLS(6), and 2-MOQLS(4) and 2-MOQLS(5) are always classical (Thms 6, 11, 12). Entangled AME(4,6) solutions fall outside this product notion, so they give no QLS mate for a classical B. The proof is order-specific case analysis (unitary patterns plus a computer screen), not a general Hall–Paige mechanism.
findings.quote: There does not exist a pair of orthogonal quantum Latin squares of order six.
findings.source: Ball & Simoens, Thirty-six quantum officers are entangled
findings.date_version: arXiv:2603.02334v1 (2 Mar 2026; only arXiv version). PRL 137, 050202 (2026) not read.
findings.scope: Orders ≤ 6, any B. Does not reach 8 or 10.

findings.claim: Ball–Simoens restate the fixed-B question as an orthonormal representation of the Latin-square-graph complement; this is their Lemma 21 for n=6, and the argument does not depend on the order [INFERENCE]. Their sound but one-sided computer screen excluded 10 of the 12 main classes. The other two, which have order-3 subsquares, needed Theorem 26. Cay(Z6) and Cay(S3) both contain order-3 subsquares [INFERENCE], so their exclusion rests on these case-specific arguments.
findings.quote: The algorithm runs for about one minute for each of the twelve Latin square graphs on 6 × 6 vertices. Only two of them yield an inconclusive True. They both have a subsquare of order three.
findings.scope: A method that could in principle be tried at n=8 or 10. Not run; parent HOLD.

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] Any QLS orthogonal to Cay(Z10) or Cay(D5) has an entry of weight ≥3 in every orthonormal basis. Reason: a unitary keeps Q orthogonal to B, and if all weights were ≤2, Lemma 13 would produce a classical mate, contradicting Hall–Paige. This is a necessary condition only.
findings.quote: If Ψ is a quantum Latin square without entries of weight three or more, then there exists a classical Latin square Ψ′ such that whenever Ψ and Φ are orthogonal, Ψ′ and Φ are orthogonal as well.
findings.source: Ball & Simoens 2603.02334v1, Lemma 13
findings.scope: Any B with no classical mate

findings.claim: Theorem 5 (n−2 MOQLS(n) are classical, n ≥ 3) reaches t=2 only for n ≤ 4. Problem 17, whether quantum ever beats classical for MOLS existence, is stated as open; the smallest open case is n=10 with t ≥ 3. No no-go, and no positive precedent either.
findings.quote: Are there numbers t and n for which there exist t MOQLS(n) but no t MOLS(n)?
findings.source: Ball & Simoens, Large sets of mutually orthogonal quantum Latin squares

findings.claim: The Frobenius-ring route covers B = Φ^(m)(i,j) = mi + j. Cay(Z10) in the j−i convention is Φ^(−1), which needs f with x ↦ f(x) + x bijective, i.e. a complete mapping of Z10, and none exists. Ψ^(f) has inner products that depend only on index differences, so the whole route lies inside the AR-invariant class [INFERENCE].
findings.quote: Let m ∈ R*. If both f(x) and x ↦ f(x) − mx are permutations of R, then Ψ^(f) and Φ^(m) are orthogonal quantum Latin squares.
findings.source: Ball & Simoens 2607.12933v2, Lemma 14 / Thm 6

findings.claim: Huang–Li's constructions need (strong) complete mappings of Z_v. Maximal-cardinality pandiagonal QLS (MCPQLS) with gcd(n,6) ≠ 1 is left undetermined. Pandiagonal in both directions is stronger than the target and would contain a Cay(Z_n) mate for even n. Open, not excluded.
findings.quote: an MCPQLS(n) exists when gcd(n,6) = 1 and n ∉ {5,7,11}. Here, an MCPQLS(5) does not exist, and the existence of MCPQLS(7), MCPQLS(11), and MCPQLS(n) with gcd(n,6) ≠ 1 remains to be determined.
findings.source: Huang & Li, The Existence of Diagonal Quantum Latin Squares with Maximum Cardinality

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] Every (Z_n,Z_n)-invariant QLS is of Fourier-permutation form ψ_{g,h}(t) = n^{−1/2} χ_t(−g) χ_{π(t)}(h). For two cells in one Cay(Z_n) class, with g'−g = h'−h = x, the inner product is n^{−1} Σ_t ζ^{x(π(t)−t)}. It vanishes for all x ≠ 0 exactly when π is an orthomorphism of Z_n, which is impossible for even n, including 8 and 10. The Huang–Li Thm 2.6, Zhang–Cao Constr. 3.3 and Ball–Simoens Ψ^(f) squares all lie in this class, so the group-structured route is provably exhausted at n=10, not just unproductive.
findings.quote: Thus the construction described in that example, which is the generalization of the construction of [18, Definition 4.1] to the case of possibly different groups G and G′, produces all (G,G′)-invariant quantum Latin squares, up to isometry.
findings.source: Árnadóttir & Roberson, Group Invariant Quantum Latin Squares (Thm 9.1, Remark 9.2)
findings.read_scope: Abstract, §1, Defs 4.1–4.3, Ex 4.4, Thm 4.5, Thms 7.5/7.7 statements, §9. No mention of Latin-square orthogonality found.

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] For non-abelian G, write U_{x,y} = τ(λ(x)* Ψ(λ(y))). Cay(D5)-orthogonality forces U_{x,y} = 0 whenever y is conjugate to x ≠ e. Summing over the class and applying Schur gives Σ_{y∈Cl(x)} U_{x,y} = (|Cl(x)|/n) Σ_χ χ(x) conj(χ^σ(x)), where σ is the degree-preserving irrep permutation induced by Ψ. At a reflection only the trivial and sign characters are nonzero, so the sum is ±2 ≠ 0. Hence no (D5,D5)-invariant mate exists, even though there are uncountably many invariant QLS.
findings.quote: Then U ∈ C^{G×G′} is a (G,G′)-transformation matrix if and only if the linear map Ψ_U : Λ_{G′} → Λ_G given by Ψ_U(λ(b)) = Σ_{a∈G} U_{a,b}λ(a) is a unitary isomorphism.
findings.source: Árnadóttir & Roberson 2501.00196v2, Thm 7.5

findings.claim: QLS that are invariant only in |⟨·,·⟩|² are not characterized. This correlation-level class includes Weyl–Heisenberg and other projective orbits. Apart from the WH10 single orbit (Grassl et al., parent-verified, not re-read here), no source rules out such Cay(Z10) mates.
findings.quote: invariance of the square of the modulus of the inner products of its entries under independent regular actions on its row and column indices. Currently, a complete characterization of such quantum Latin squares seems out of reach.
findings.source: Árnadóttir & Roberson 2501.00196v2, §1

findings.claim: Classical background: if Cay(G) has a transversal or mate, its Sylow 2-subgroup is trivial or non-cyclic, and no cyclic group of even order has a transversal. So Z10, D5 and Z8 have no classical mate.
findings.quote: (iii) There exists a latin square orthogonal to LG. ... (v) The Sylow 2-subgroups of G are trivial or non-cyclic. ... Paige [43] showed that (i) implies (iv). Hall and Paige [28] then showed that (iv) implies (v).
findings.source: Wanless, Transversals in Latin squares (survey)

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] The parent's FCO family q_ij(t) = ζ^{tj+π(t)ρ(i)}/√n gives a Cay(Z_n) mate exactly when H_{i,t} = ζ^{it+ρ(i)π(t)} is Hadamard. That holds exactly when (Γ_π, Λ_ρ) is a spectral pair in Z_n^2, which is the same as a log-Hadamard matrix of mod-n rank ≤2 whose two factor columns are permutations.
findings.quote: If L ⊂ Ĝ is a spectrum of A (regarded as a d × k matrix), then H := (1/N) L·A is log-Hadamard (where the matrix multiplication can be taken mod N).
findings.source: Kolountzakis & Matolcsi, Complex Hadamard matrices and the spectral set conjecture
findings.scope: Dictionary only. States no permutation-graph result.

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] Cross-check of the parent's n=7 count. IMP Thm 3.3 (equidistribution) means that in a spectral pair, D(E) avoids the perpendiculars of D(A), so |D(E)| + |D(A)| ≤ p+1. Rédei's bound then forces π or ρ to be affine. With π(0) = ρ(0) = 0 the count is 2(p−1)N_p − (p−1)(p−2), where N_p is the number of normalized complete mappings of Z_p. N_7 = 133/7 = 19 gives 198, exactly the parent's n=7 count. This is an independent analytic check of the enumeration at n=7.
findings.quote: If E is a spectral set in Z²_p, p an odd prime, then E is either a point, a graph set of order p or the whole space and hence tiles Z²_p in all cases.
findings.source: Iosevich, Mayeli, Pakianathan, The Fuglede Conjecture holds in Z_p × Z_p
findings.read_scope: Full v1 text (Thm 3.2, Thm 3.3, Prop 3.5, Cor 3.6)

findings.claim: Rédei's bound used in the n=7 cross-check.
findings.quote: Rédei [11] proved that when q is an odd prime, any non-affine function determines at least (q + 3)/2 directions, so this is the best we can do.
findings.source: Ball & Simoens 2607.12933v2, §4.1

findings.claim: Transversal counts of cyclic squares: Z7 has 133, so N_7 = 19. The list view does not show the sequence title. Identifying it as cyclic-square transversal counts rests on memory plus agreement with Wanless Table 3 (37851 at n=11).
findings.source: OEIS A006717

findings.claim: Fuglede's conjecture holds in Z_pq^2, which includes Z10^2 with p=2, q=5, and size-pq spectral sets tile by a cyclic subgroup of order pq. Graphs of permutations always tile by the vertical subgroup, so this does NOT give the FCO no-go. No lemma in the paper constrains spectra to avoid permutation shapes.
findings.quote: Theorem 1.2. Fuglede's conjecture holds for Z²_p × Z²_q ≅ Z_pq × Z_pq, where q and p are different primes. ... Therefore S must tile by a Z_p × Z_q subgroup.
findings.source: Fallon, Kiss, Somlai, Spectral sets and tiles in Z_p^2 × Z_q^2
findings.scope: Spectral ⟺ tile; does not address the spectrum's shape

findings.claim: [INFERENCE] The target object is a rank-one, dimension-n quantum perfect matching of the 3-partite Latin hypergraph: projections |q_ij⟩⟨q_ij| whose row, column and B-class sums are all I. Higher-rank quantum perfect matchings neither imply nor exclude it. Elsewhere, quantum perfect matchings exist where classical ones cannot; this is only a weak analogy for headroom. The paper has no Latin-hypergraph result.
findings.quote: In the quantum setting, we show that complete graphs K_n with odd n ≥ 7 have quantum perfect matchings. ... we prove that deciding quantum perfect matchings in hypergraphs is undecidable
findings.source: Cui, Mančinska, Nezhadi, Roberson, Quantum Perfect Matchings
findings.read_scope: §§1–3, §6 headings; grep found no Latin/transversal mentions

findings.claim: Confirms the small-order picture; the smallest known pair with both squares at maximal cardinality is order 64.
findings.quote: Moreover, the results of Ball and Simoens [3] imply that every orthogonal pair of order 3, 4 or 5 is classical, and that no orthogonal pair of order 6 exists.
findings.source: Lv, Zhang, Cao, Orthogonal QLS with maximal cardinality from full-rank factorizations

findings.claim: The first non-classical orthogonal pair (Musto–Vicary) has order 9; I did not check its partner's mate status. Every construction whose classical partner I could identify (Huang–Li, Zhang–Cao, Ball–Simoens Thm 6) uses a group or linear table that has classical mates [INFERENCE]. I found no QLS mate for any Latin square without a classical mate.
findings.quote: We give the first example of a pair of orthogonal quantum Latin squares which are not equivalent to a pair of classical Latin squares. (Example 5 and Proposition 13.)
findings.source: Musto & Vicary, Orthogonality for quantum Latin isometry squares

findings.claim: Forward-citation screen. Zhang–Cao: 0 indexed citations. The 7 INSPIRE records citing Ball–Simoens (36 officers) cover real AME(4,6) states, AME classification, RQLS and large sets; none treats fixed-B quantum mates. math.CO coverage in these indexes is incomplete.
findings.quote: title: Resolvable quantum Latin squares with maximal cardinality; publication_date: 2026-08-29; cited_by_count: 0
findings.source: OpenAlex and INSPIRE (refersto:recid:3125388, 3198253, 2864467, 3180352)
findings.scope: A search miss is not novelty

theorem_comparison.target: Unit vectors q_ij ∈ C^10 whose rows, columns and B-symbol classes are all orthonormal bases, for B = Cay(Z10) (B = j−i) or Cay(D5), with no symmetry assumed. Equivalently: a QLS orthogonal (tensor-ONB sense) to classical B; an orthonormal representation in C^n of B's Latin-square graph (adjacent ⇒ orthogonal); a rank-one, dimension-n quantum perfect matching of B's 3-partite hypergraph [INFERENCE].
theorem_comparison.scope_ladder: Four levels, and results do not transfer between them: (a) a QLS alone (maximal ones exist for n ≥ 4); (b) a QLS plus one classical partner — this target, which Zhang–Cao call 1-RQLS; (c) two quantum MOQLS (smallest known with both maximal: order 64); (d) entangled AME(4,n) pairs. Example: AME(4,6) exists but 2-MOQLS(6) does not, and classical 2-MOLS(10) exist while fixed-B mates of Cay(Z10) remain unknown.
covered_by_sources: n−2 MOQLS are classical (irrelevant at t=2, n=10)
WH10 single orbit (Grassl et al. via parent)
restricted_classes_excluded_INFERENCE: Whole AR (Z_n,Z_n)-invariant class for even n, including every Huang–Li, Zhang–Cao and Ball–Simoens construction
FCO family for n = 2p (proof below). n=8 FCO = 0 rests on the parent's enumeration only.
theorem_comparison.not_covered: Unrestricted fixed-B for Cay(Z10), Cay(D5), Cay(Z8), and any group with cyclic nontrivial Sylow 2-subgroup. No theorem found. Modulus-invariant (projective) classes beyond the WH10 single orbit are also unexcluded.
theorem_comparison.FCO_no_go_n_eq_2p_INFERENCE_unreviewed: Setting: n = 2p, p an odd prime. FCO gives a mate exactly when H H* = nI for H_{i,t} = ζ_n^{it+ρ(i)π(t)}. (1) CRT: ζ_n^x = (−1)^x ω^{cx}, with ω = ζ_p and c = 2^{−1} mod p. For a row pair let a = i'−i, b = ρ(i')−ρ(i), E_t = at + bπ(t). Then Σ_t ζ^{E_t} = Σ_v (M⁺_v − M⁻_v) ω^{cv}, where M^±_v counts the t with E_t ≡ v mod p and E_t even (+) or odd (−). Since Φ_p is the minimal polynomial, the sum vanishes iff M⁺_v − M⁻_v = κ for every v, with pκ = #even − #odd and |κ| ≤ 2. (2) Every permutation ρ has some pair with a and b both odd. For that pair Σ_t (−1)^{t+π(t)} = 4k − 2p ≡ 2 mod 4, where k = #{t even : π(t) even}. This forces κ = ±2, so k = 0 or k = p: π keeps or swaps the two parity classes. The columns of H/√n are orthonormal too, so the same holds for ρ. (3) Hence every row pair has (a,b) ≡ (0,0) or (1,1) mod 2, and E_t has constant parity. Then κ = ±2, so the values E_t mod p hit every residue exactly twice. Put P_i = (i, ρ(i)) mod p and Q_t = (t, π(t)) mod p; then E_t ≡ (P_{i'} − P_i)·Q_t. (4) If P_{i'} = P_i, then E_t ≡ 0 for all t, a contradiction. So the 2p points P_i are distinct, and since 2p > p they determine every direction of F_p^2. That makes the Fourier transform of Q's multiplicity function (total mass 2p) vanish at every nonzero frequency, so the multiplicity is constant 2/p, which is not an integer. Contradiction. This covers n = 6, 10, 14, 22, … It does not cover n = 8 or n = 2·(odd composite). Consistent with Ball–Simoens at n=6 and with the parent's n=10 enumeration.
theorem_comparison.AR_class_derivation_INFERENCE: See findings 9–10. The abelian case reduces to an orthomorphism of Z_n. D5 fails the class-sum character identity at reflections (value ±2).
theorem_comparison.parity_identity_INFERENCE: The proposal's identity Σ_{j<i} P_ij = ((n−1)/2) I, grouped by rows into R_i (a rank-i projection), already excludes n=4. Indeed (3/2)I − R_3 has full rank, yet rank(R_1 + R_2) ≤ 3. So the proposal's 'not an obstruction for n ≥ 4' is wrong at n=4, though consistent with the import. At n=6 the row-grouped identity alone can be satisfied: use three C² blocks — two of type {R_5 = I; R_2, R_3, R_4 a trine; R_1 = 0} and one of type {R_4 = I; R_1, R_3, R_5 a trine; R_2 = 0}. So it gives no general even-n obstruction.
theorem_comparison.pilot_relevant_constraints: Any verified v=10 endpoint must lie outside the WH10 single orbit, the AR-invariant class and the FCO family. It must also have an entry of weight ≥3 in every basis. Cay(Z8) is the smallest even cyclic case with no unrestricted no-go: the AR class is excluded [INFERENCE], and FCO = 0 by parent enumeration only.

output.significance: Calibrated as follows. The literature gives no obstruction for the unrestricted fixed-B target, so headroom is 'unexcluded but unprecedented'. The restricted exclusions I derived are corollary-level consequences of AR + Hall–Paige. The FCO n=2p proof is a short specialist argument (cyclotomic relation plus pigeonhole), at most a modest extension; it may be folklore among Fuglede specialists. I make no priority claim. A verified positive Cay(Z10) or Cay(D5) mate would be potentially substantive specialist work: it would be a QLS mate for a mate-less B, which I found in no screened source, and it would bear on Ball–Simoens-type 'quantum beats classical' questions. 'Major' is not established. For the pilot, these restricted no-gos explain the negative structured searches, but they cannot be cited as evidence against the unrestricted model.
counterpoints: Against headroom: orders 2, 4 and 6 are fully negative for every B.
Against headroom: every structured class at v=10 is negative (WH10 single orbit, AR-invariant, FCO), and there is no positive precedent for any mate-less B.
Against headroom: the n=6 exclusion of both group tables relied on subsquare-specific arguments. Cay(Z10) and Cay(D5) are 5-step type with order-5 subsquares, and no analogue is known.
For headroom: no general quantum mechanism replaces Hall–Paige. The classical parity identity alone fails to obstruct at n=6, as the block example shows.
For headroom: Lemma 13 only forces weight-≥3 entries, which generic solutions have anyway.
For headroom: modulus-invariant classes are uncharacterized (AR).
For headroom: quantum matchings beat classical ones in other settings (K_n with n odd ≥ 7).
For headroom: Ball–Simoens Problem 17 is explicitly open.
Neutral: the naive equation-versus-parameter count gives no evidence either way.
